Task 18 on branch resplit-keep (this worktree). Do not run `next start` or
`next dev`. Do not read or print secret values; never create .env files. Never
run `npm run build:book` (it calls paid APIs). Stay inside pipeline/ and core/
plus the docs named below.

Problem: in pipeline/resplit.ts the per-scene worker inside `runPool` throws
`scene ${scene.id} titles do not cover the split ranges` when Muse's
resplit_titles answer does not match the planned ranges. One bad Muse answer
aborts the whole book build and wastes the run's spend. A Muse call that
rejects (network/HTTP error) in the resplit_decision ask or the resplit_titles
call has the same effect. A Jev window failure, by contrast, already keeps
the scene whole and records the id in `window_failures`.

Change (smallest diff):
1. Treat both cases like the Jev window failure: keep the original scene whole
   (the worker returns null), record it, continue with the other scenes.
   Record into a new provenance array `provenance.resplit.muse_failures:
   { from: string; reason: string }[]` (reason: short, e.g. "titles do not
   cover the split ranges" or the error message truncated to 200 chars; never
   include request bodies or keys). Spend already tracked for that scene stays
   counted. Do not wrap the whole worker in a broad try/catch: catch only
   around the Muse calls and the title/range check. The post-pool duplicate-id
   and coverage checks must still throw (those are real bugs).
2. Update the file header comment if needed and the resplit provenance shape
   in docs (grep docs/ for `window_failures` and add `muse_failures` next to
   it in one short clause).
3. Tests in pipeline/resplit.test.ts, reusing setupDir and the fake clients:
   (a) titles answer with wrong ranges for one scene: runResplit resolves,
   that scene keeps its original id and range, the other scene still splits,
   muse_failures has one entry with its id, coverage still valid;
   (b) titles call rejects: same outcome;
   (c) resplit_decision ask rejects: scene kept whole, recorded.
   Normal-path tests must stay unchanged and green.

A normal full run's behaviour and output must not change except the new
(empty) `muse_failures: []` array in the resplit provenance. Do not touch
data/books/oz.

Run npm test, npm run typecheck, npm run check:isolation, npm run
check:secrets, npm run test:hooks, npm run check:size. Commit through the
hook with message "Keep a scene whole when Muse resplit answers fail" and
trailer "Co-authored-by: Muse Code (Meta) <muse-code@agents.noreply.invalid>".

29|`final_left`/`final_right` from the re-classified parts,

31|emotion and folded back), `rejected` (Muse declined), and
32|`window_failures` (Jev failed, scene left whole).

36|One static route per scene (`app/leer/[sceneId]`, `dynamicParams`
37|false); `/` redirects to the first scene. The layout mounts the music
38|container once and passes slim metadata for all scenes: id, chapter,
39|and emotion triple only. Each scene page builds its view with
40|`buildSceneView` and ships only that scene's text, its chapter title,
41|and neighbor ids. Sub-pages come from `paginateScene`, which closes a
42|page when the next paragraph would pass 250 words or the line budget
43|(`FIRST_PAGE_LINES` 16 on page one, `LINES_PER_PAGE` 17 after, each
44|paragraph costing `ceil(chars / CHARS_PER_LINE)` lines with
45|`CHARS_PER_LINE` 68), split at paragraph boundaries. The pager moves sub-pages in client state and
46|pushes routes with `router.push`, never `<Link>`; going back lands on
47|the previous scene's last sub-page through a one-shot client flag, never
48|a URL param, so prerendered pages stay static. The client never
49|receives other scenes' text, titles, or summaries. The progress line
50|reads `Chapter 1 · The Cyclone`, a spaced separator, then `Scene 1 of 4
51|· Page 1 of 3` as two spans on one line. Book type is 1.1875rem / 1.7
52|with no paragraph gaps and a 1.5em first-line indent on following
53|paragraphs. The word budget stays the upper bound and the line budget
54|keeps every sub-page inside 1280×800 without scroll.

58|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 3, fetched
59|by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
60|ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
61|several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so. A version 2
62|manifest migrates inline to one implicit `default` soundtrack of style
63|`orchestral`.
64|
65|`MusicManifest = { version, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`.
66|`StyleInfo = { id, name }` where `id` is a lowercase slug and `name` is
67|the display name. `Soundtrack = { id, name, style }` plus
68|optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
69|intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
70|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
71|loop), `endSec` (default the media end, where the track stops or loops),
72|`gainDb` (default 0, a loudness trim in dB, in -24..12),
73|`loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
74|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
75|`sourceUrl` (https only). `durationSec` is the playable length: the
76|segment end (or the file end) minus `startSec`. `startSec` and `endSec`
77|are absolute media times with `startSec < endSec`; `endSec` stays within
78|`startSec + durationSec`. The player scales volume by the track gain and
79|ends or loops at `effectiveEnd`, the earlier of `endSec` and the loaded

# Durable Test Collateral

Verification is part of the delivered project when it can prevent the same
behavior from breaking again. Use the project's existing framework and
conventions.

Loading this skill does not mean the current turn asked for the change. While you
are still investigating — explaining existing behavior, or answering a design
question the user raised — use commands that only read and leave the repository
unmodified, tests included.

## Scale to the task

Skip the failing-test-first workflow below when the change is tiny and leaves
program logic alone (a typo, a text or style tweak, a config value, or a version
pin), when the work is a throwaway prototype or a standalone one-file script or
page, when the request adds features to a project you created earlier in this
session, or when the user asks for speed or a quick result. A quick direct check
of the changed behavior is enough there; if you add no maintained test, say so in
the report. A user request for tests anywhere in the session, or a
specification that makes tests a deliverable, still applies.

Any other bug fix or behavior change keeps the workflow at its smallest: one
focused failing test, the fix, that test passing, and, when a broad run is
required, one broad run after the final edit. A report that something already
built behaves wrongly is a bug fix, even when it comes with feature requests.

Before a test run that may take more than a minute or two, tell the user in one
line what runs and why. If you poll it, post a short status line between polls;
never poll a long run silently.

## Keep the check with the project

For a bug fix or behavior change, add or update the smallest maintained test in
the repository's normal test layout that exercises the changed behavior. If a
specification makes a reusable suite or test category a deliverable, implement
that suite instead of treating it as private verification.

An inline interpreter command, heredoc, scratch script, temporary-directory
test, demo, or manual probe may help diagnose the problem, but it does not
replace the maintained test. Keep a useful self-authored test unless the user
explicitly asks for a disposable probe.

Do not add a new test framework solely to satisfy this skill. If the repository
has no maintained harness and the request does not require one, disclose when
durable coverage would be disproportionate or infeasible and use the narrowest
honest verification instead.

On a later turn, update the maintained test even when the old suite remains
green and the user does not repeat the test request. Cover the new behavior,
not merely an unrelated cleanup in the test file.

## Prove the maintained check

Observe the authentic failure before the implementation change when it is safe
and runnable. Then make the smallest implementation change and run the focused
maintained test after the final relevant source or test edit.

Do not weaken or delete a real failing test to obtain green. Fix the product,
or explain why the test's expectation is wrong before changing that
expectation. Do not repeat an unchanged check solely to collect evidence.

Run a broad or full suite only when the user, a repository gate, or
proportionate risk requires it, and then once, after the final edit, rather
than after each intermediate edit. A focused regression test comes first; broad
proof does not substitute for missing focused coverage.

Before deciding what a repository gate requires, read what the repository
declares it runs: its CI workflow, its test entry points, and its root-level
scripts listed with hidden entries included. A suite the project itself runs
over this change is a gate, not an optional extra, and a suite that skips
itself when its data is absent is not a green result.

A runner is unavailable only after you tried to make it available. When the
repository ships the command that fetches or builds the missing fixture,
corpus, or toolchain, run that command once and then run the gate. Report the
gate unavailable only when that attempt itself failed, and say what failed.

If the real runner is unavailable but the focused test can still be authored
honestly, leave the focused test in the repository and say it was not run. Do
not fabricate a passing result.

</skill-body>
</read-skill-result>

# Prepare-commit-msg: add the Muse Code co-author trailer idempotently.

# Git source-control safety

The working tree belongs to the user. Make the change, leave it visible, and
let them decide what becomes history.

## Never without an explicit ask

The user must have asked for that exact write in this session, in their own
words. An explicit request to create a new commit counts anywhere in the user's
own task text, but it is not a request to amend, push, or tag. Finishing a task
without that request does not authorize a history write.

- `commit`, `commit --amend`, `push`, `tag`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`,
  `merge`, branch deletion, `reset --hard`, path restore, and `clean -f` all
  require an explicit ask.
- Never publish merely because publication would be useful.

## Before an authorized discard

Recovery is insurance, not authorization. A save never expands what the user
allowed you to delete or overwrite.

When the user explicitly authorized an operation that may discard or broadly
overwrite workspace changes, and the workspace is an ordinary Git checkout:

1. After `muse.read_skill` gives the physical Git skill package path, run:

   ```bash
   bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh save before-discard
   ```

2. Keep the printed `refs/tbh/recovery/...` value in your handoff, then perform
   only the exact authorized operation.
3. If the save fails or the workspace is unsupported, stop before destruction
   and ask the user.

To recover that saved tree later, run:

```bash
bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh restore <recovery-ref>
```

Restore first saves the current workspace, leaves HEAD, branch, and the real
index in place, and restores the selected snapshot into the worktree. The ref
also retains distinct staged bytes when the same path had later worktree edits.
Read those staged bytes with `git show '<recovery-ref>^2:<path>'`; the recovery
commit's second parent is the saved index tree. Ignored files are not saved;
restore refuses an ignored-path collision rather than overwrite data it could
not save. Use only the exact printed ref, not a revision expression.

## Always fine

Read-only inspection such as `status`, `log`, `show`, `diff`, `blame`,
`branch -v`, `show-ref`, `rev-parse`, `for-each-ref`, and `merge-base` is fine.
Staging named files to inspect `diff --cached`, and a temporary stash around a
tool that requires a clean tree, are also fine when the original state is put
back afterward.

## The rest

- Do not use a broad add in a tree you did not clean; name the files you changed.
- Do not initialize a repository inside vendored, build, data, or existing
  source-control trees.
- Do not create or edit `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude` to hide the user's
  files, and do not stash the user's files (including `stash push -u`) to make
  `git status` look clean. "Leave the working tree clean", "tidy up", and
  similar phrasing do not authorize committing, pushing, ignoring, excluding,
  stashing, or deleting the user's files; clean up only scratch you created
  and say the user's files remain.
- Do not hand-edit generated files; change their source of truth.
- Scratch repositories under a temporary directory are yours to experiment in.

## Locks and corrupt state

A Git lock usually means another process is writing. Never kill the holder on
your own initiative. Wait, inspect the holder read-only, use that tool's normal
stop mechanism, or report the block. Never delete a lock without proving no
live process owns it, and never respond to index corruption by deleting state
and committing anyway.

Never commit or push while status reports changes you did not make and cannot
explain.

## If you already made an unwanted write

Say so plainly and stop. Do not attempt more history surgery without direction.
